Guide

Finding fees that were never recorded at all

For the owner and the principal About 6 minutes

Most anti-fraud advice for schools is about receipts: number them, never delete them, keep the book. That advice is right and it catches one kind of problem. It cannot catch the other kind, and the other kind is bigger.

The two kinds, and why one is invisible

Under-recording is when a payment is entered for less than was taken. A parent pays Rs 5,800, the receipt says Rs 3,800. Gapless receipt numbers and a copy of the receipt going to the parent catch this, because two records of the same event exist and they disagree.

Non-recording is when the payment is never entered at all. A parent pays Rs 5,800 in cash, no receipt is written, and the money does not reach the drawer. There is now exactly one record of the event, in the parent's memory, and nothing in the school's books to compare it against. Your receipt book is perfect. Your day book balances. The month's collection is simply smaller than it should have been, and nothing in the system knows what "should have been" is.

A perfectly balanced set of books proves that what was written down is consistent. It says nothing at all about what was not written down.

The check that does work

Compare what the roll says should have been billed against what was actually collected, class by class, and look at the difference. That is it. The power of it is that the expected figure comes from a completely different source than the collected figure: the roll and the fee structure, not the receipt book.

For one class the arithmetic is:

LineWhere it comes fromExample
Pupils on the rollThe admission register34
Monthly fee for the classThe fee structureRs 3,750
Approved concessionsThe discount registerRs 5,200
Expected34 x 3,750 minus 5,200Rs 122,300
Collected this monthThe receipt bookRs 96,000
GapExpected minus collectedRs 26,300

A gap is a question, not an accusation

This matters, and getting it wrong will cost you a good clerk. In every school we have looked at, most of the gap is one of these, and none of them is theft:

  • Pupils who left and were never marked as gone. They are still on the roll, so they are still being billed, and no money will ever arrive. This is usually the single largest slice.
  • Concessions granted verbally. The principal told a family to pay half and nobody wrote it in the discount register, so the expected figure is too high by the amount of the kindness.
  • Families who are simply behind. Genuine arrears, already known to the office, correctly recorded.
  • A wrong fee amount on the class. The structure says Rs 3,750 and the school has been charging Rs 3,500 since the last increase was agreed.

Work down that list before you think about the fifth possibility. And when you find one of the first four, the fix is a record: mark the leaver as left, write the concession in the register, correct the fee amount. Each one you fix makes the next month's gap a sharper instrument.

The ghost check, which needs no software

Take the list of pupils being billed this month. Take the attendance register for the same month. Any pupil on the first list who appears on no day of the second is worth a five minute conversation. They have almost certainly left. You are billing a family that has moved on, and your expected figure is carrying money that will never arrive.

How often to run it

Monthly, at the same point in the month, and write the figure down. One month's gap tells you very little. Six months of gaps tells you whether the number is drifting, and in which class, which is the thing you actually want to know.

How this works in The School Manager

The expected against collected table is a screen, computed from the roll and the fee structure rather than typed in, with the shortfall per class and the ghost check beside it. Concessions cannot be granted without an approver and a reason, which removes the second cause above entirely, and a leaver marked as left stops being billed the same day.

It is worth being clear that no software can find non-recording on its own. What it can do is compute the expected figure honestly, from a source the person taking the cash does not control, and put the two numbers next to each other every month without anybody having to remember.
